speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Allow me to explain the main amendments and new provisions of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One growing area of concern of my Ministry is with the state of public cleanliness in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over the years, Singapore has earned a reputation as a clean city.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is something that many Singaporeans are proud of and many of us view a clean environment as an important part of the Singapore identity, as reflected in some of the polls that have been conducted.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, maintaining a clean Singapore cannot be left to cleaners alone.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Members would have read in the news of how festival-goers of Laneway Music Festival in 2015 and 2016 left the venue littered with trash despite the fervent efforts of volunteers from the Traceless Movement who went around the event venue to pick up trash strewn on the floor.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Just a few weeks ago, members would have read in the news about the large amount of litter that was left behind after the countdown to 2016 at Marina Bay.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many concerned members of public have also provided feedback on how to improve the situation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: During a recent radio discussion, some callers pressed for harsher penalties while many more said that there should be a focus of creating a culture of community ownership.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over the years, the Government has stepped up enforcement against littering.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have also taken a tougher stance towards littering by imposing stiffer penalties for recalcitrant offenders.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ultimately, public cleanliness should be the outcome of the intrinsic values and habits of our people and not just the result of cleaning services and enforcing rules.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, it is not even related to the number of waste bins we provide for the convenience of the public.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Members who have been to Japan would agree that the level of public cleanliness there is much higher than Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The public areas in Japan are cleaner not because there is a large army of cleaners, but because of the Japanese people's habits and social norms.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, in many public places, bins are scarce in Japan.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is something that we can strive to emulate, by creating a culture of community ownership so that everyone takes responsibility in maintaining high standards of public cleanliness and hygiene and treat public places like their own homes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have started this journey with a good number of volunteers who are passionate about the cleanliness of our public spaces and are active in helping us keep them clean.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As part of the Keep Singapore Clean movement, the Public Hygiene Council partnered residents, schools, businesses and community groups to turn our community spaces into "Bright Spots".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are essentially shared spaces adopted by stakeholders who take ownership of the area's cleanliness and hygiene conditions and lead by example to promote good social norms.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To date, our CVs have collectively engaged more than 2,500 litterbugs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I understand that the public has shown an interest in playing a more active role in keeping our environment clean.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Last year, my Ministry announced during the Committee of Supply debate that we will expand the CV programme so as to allow members of the public to take greater ownership of the environment.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Specifically, we will allow individuals to join the expanded CV programme without having to be affiliated to a recognised environmental group and empower them to engage offenders for a wider range of offences beyond littering.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will broaden the pool who can be tapped on to join the programme.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In addition, we will allow CVs to have the option of participating in advocacy, outreach and educational activities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Through the expanded CV programme, we hope to see more CVs taking ownership of the cleanliness and hygiene conditions of existing Bright Spots numbering more than 520 and lead by example to promote good social norms.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To this end, clause 5(c) of the Bill inserts a new section 16A into the NEA Act to allow any individual, including volunteers, to be appointed as an auxiliary officer to assist NEA in performing its functions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clause 5(h) inserts a new section 42A into the NEA Act to specifically empower the Chief Executive of NEA to authorise, in writing, an auxiliary officer to exercise all or any of the powers of enforcement conferred on an officer or employee of NEA by the NEA Act or any environmental written law, in relation to an offence under the NEA Act or that environmental written law.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clause 5(b) defines "environmental written law" to mean any written law administered by NEA, the Director-General of Environmental Protection or the Director-General of Public Health.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clauses 2, 3 and 4 make consequential amendments to the CVPA, EPMA and EPHA in order to allow an auxiliary officer to be appointed as an "authorised officer" for those Acts, and thereby exercise the powers of enforcement conferred on authorised officers under those Acts.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Next, enabling auxiliary police officers to exercise powers of enforcement in relation to environmental offences.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under the Police Force Act, an auxiliary police officer (APO) can assist a Government department or statutory body with the enforcement of certain offences.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: NEA currently engages APOs appointed under the Police Force Act to enforce certain environmental offences such as spitting and littering.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This aligns the position under the EPHA and CVPA on the appointment of APOs as authorised officers with the corresponding positions under certain other Acts administered by NEA, such as the EPMA and the Energy Conservation Act.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These cameras help to deter abusive behaviour by offenders towards NEA officers, protect them against allegations of unprofessional conduct, as well as remind them to abide by the relevant operational protocol in the execution of their duties.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This Bill will allow passionate individuals to take greater community ownership of our environment and better complement NEA's enforcement efforts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Undoubtedly, without volunteers, many projects and plans would not be able to achieve the desired results.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The volunteers are a unique group of people who are always on the ground, doing their part for the community without much fanfare.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Most importantly, they are a positive influence on the people around them to volunteer for the good of the community.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am delighted to note that the amendment to the existing NEA Act is looking towards expanding the Community Volunteer scheme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans are a more civic-minded lot and I believe there is a lot of potential in the CV scheme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, I pledge my full support to expand the CV scheme so that individuals too can be appointed as CVs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Personally, I am a great believer of community volunteerism.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To address the littering problem, my grassroots team and I have been organising monthly litter-picking exercises.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These involve residents and students in our neighbourhood estates.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When I mooted this monthly litter-picking in 2012, there was a lot of initial scepticism.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I was asked, "Bee Wah, are you sure or not?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What if you go and pick litter, no one follow you?" I am glad that every month there are about 100 to 200 residents, students, nurses from Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, Lions members, as well as residents beyond Nee Soon South, those who care about environment, come and join us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I deeply appreciate their contributions and I am sure some of these residents will be keen to volunteer under the CV scheme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Litter has been a constant thorn faced by many developed countries and densely populated cities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A great number of annual anti-litter picking campaigns are held worldwide: Clean Up the World, Don't Mess with Texas, Keep Britain Tidy, Keep Australia Beautiful, Hong Kong is The Face of Litter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are just a few memorable ones out of the many national and localised campaigns held in countries across the global map.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, we have our very own Keep Singapore Clean campaign.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And in Nee Soon South we have our own HABIT.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are numerous NGOs world-wide supporting community clean-up efforts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These campaigns certainly bear some weight in keeping the littering problem at bay.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, we will have to look further for more comprehensive solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that, eventually, it will be progressed, like what is happening in Japan and Taiwan, where every student not just clean their own classroom, they clean the school compound, they wash the toilets, they sort out the litter and they do not have cleaners in the schools.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This not only helps to save resources and generate more efficiency, but as a ground-up initiative, it will have more social impact.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It will foster social norm and I hope that it will remind would-be litterbugs that there are eyes around them; there are people who care and love the environment watching them all the time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Since 2002, the UK has roped in volunteers to become Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs), who help support front line officers by dealing with minor offences and anti-social behaviour, including littering.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They play a crucial role in neighbourhood and police work, freeing up time and resources for the police to focus on other more crucial crimes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are paid a token salary; however, there are now plans to engage unpaid volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Mumbai, volunteers could fine litterbugs, a move welcomed by the volunteers who bemoaned apathetic litterbugs that refused to heed warnings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These volunteers are armed with ID cards and arm bands as identification proof.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But as with all "super volunteers", the greatest challenge remains in finding volunteers with the relevant skills, commitment and integrity to carry out their duties.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Passion is important, but it does not necessarily equate suitability.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Adequate training and resources will have to be invested in this programme.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe there would be stringent screening of those who want to volunteer under this scheme so that what attracts them is their passion to serve and not the appetite for authority or power.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, we have to think of how to protect these volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I fully support the use of body-worn cameras and, besides that, tough punishment have to be meted out for those who abuse the law enforcement officers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But like any work, be it full-time or voluntary, people must be properly motivated and managed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Early this year, there have been some opinion pieces in the TODAY newspaper discussing the act of incentivising volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think volunteer management is something we need to consider very carefully in our long-term plan to recruit and empower more volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we maintain the motivation in our volunteers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we keep that flame alive year after year?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Job satisfaction, the feeling of being wanted, the thought of having made a difference, their love for environment are powerful emotions that spur the volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Volunteers need to feel appreciated to continue their work or they will move on to other causes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One thing can be for sure, we should never reduce volunteerism to just a dollar value.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I certainly believe that more can be done to raise the social profile of volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When we hear someone say they are volunteering for the United Nations, or the SPCA, or a nursing home or orphanage, our first reaction is often to express admiration for the person.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because we feel that he or she is directly contributing to the cause of improving and helping the less fortunate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But for littering and smoking causes, often people cannot visualise the impact they are contributing to the environment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many think that this is not their job.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And some even labelled their friends or volunteers, "They are kaypoh." The inclination is to shower less admiration for their work done.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, employers should pay more attention to job applicants who are volunteering for good causes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Bosses, top management, CEOs and community leaders should lead by example.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Generating more public awareness will not only help to promote the importance of environmental volunteerism, but also give them the recognition they truly deserve.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope to see this number reduced in due course.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   	The Ministry of Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) proposed that we should train more volunteers so that they can enforce the law to deal with litterbugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I feel that to maintain the passion of these volunteers is not easy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Contributions from Community Volunteers are not as noticeable as volunteers who help the vulnerable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The authority should explore how to increase environment awareness in the society and encourage the community to express gratitude towards these volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the employers, bosses, CEOs and community leaders can set an example and encourage their subordinates to care for the environment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, I hope that everyone in our society can do his or her part for the environment and reduce our reliance on cleaners.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party supports the principle that underpins this Bill, which is to rope community volunteers, preserve and upkeep the environment and the cleanliness of our home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is the philosophy that appears to underpin the NEA's CV scheme introduced a mere three years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under this scheme, volunteers replace the presence of NEA officers on the ground and promote a more educative approach with lawbreakers while, nonetheless, retaining the authority to take down an individual's details before forwarding them to NEA for further review and investigation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These volunteers act to supplement NEA officers who cannot be everywhere all the time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This represents a manifest escalation of the concept of not just the current CV scheme, but crucially the very concept of volunteerism as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill also seeks Parliament's approval to extend extensive powers ordinarily held by state employees to volunteers and for the Chief Executive of the NEA to limit these powers accordingly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, Parliament's role is relegated to that of a mere rubber stamp.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have five queries on the potential appointment of volunteers as auxiliary officers for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2012, the NEA launched a volunteer programme which I mentioned earlier, and trained a group of volunteers from various NGOs, namely, the Public Hygiene Council, Waterways Watch Society, Singapore Kindness Movement, Singapore Environmental Council and the Cat Welfare Society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand from the Minister's Second Reading speech that new organisations will now be included in this pool.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm what criteria must a new organisation fulfil to be considered?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Pioneer Generation Package allows for every Pioneer Generation ambassador to receive a $10 allowance when they visit each Pioneer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can come up to be a significant sum for a volunteer and I understand that some volunteers have earned a few hundred dollars a month visiting Pioneers, a sum that goes well beyond defraying the cost of food and transport.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How much will a volunteer receive for each assignment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the payout determined by the number of volunteer hours or the number of summons issued or some other determinant?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, volunteers with enforcement powers: will it upset our multi-racial community?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from the uncomfortable nexus between volunteerism and paid work, has NEA considered the behavioural aspects of volunteer enforcers on the wider community?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With volunteers' extended enforcement powers, neighbours can potentially sign up as innocuous and well-meaning volunteers but who will then have to exercise their enforcement powers to summon some friends and neighbours in some cases while issuing a warning in other cases and then, exercising compassion in yet another series of cases depending on each situation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The flexibility which enforcement officers are endowed with has a real risk of inadvertently promoting a toxic environment in our communities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It can be construed by non-volunteer neighbours as blatant favouritism or worse, as an attempt by some volunteers to create a power or patronage networks that cannot be effectively policed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many auxiliary officers and volunteers does the Ministry have in mind to assist NEA for the tasks at hand?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does NEA plan to deploy these volunteers and will they be evenly spread out across Singapore or concentrated in areas which attract a large number of volunteers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister assure this House that there would be an even deployment of volunteers with the greatly scoped powers across the country to ensure that no areas are left out by a shortage of volunteers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the alternative if there are not enough volunteers in one particular area, will there be a corresponding increase in the number of NEA or auxiliary officers deployed to areas where the volunteer pool is small?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If this is not done, in all likelihood, there may be pockets of areas in Singapore that remain problematic hotspots.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the Minister should consider a global approach to deployment of NEA officers, auxiliary officers and volunteers with properly scoped powers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does NEA intend to require volunteers to work with Town Councils to jointly identify problematic areas?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If volunteers are drawn from the People's Association's Grassroots Organisations (PA GROs), how are they envisaged to work with Opposition Town Councils?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is timely in view of the growing problem of littering.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is consistent with a survey by NEA in 2010 which found that one third of Singaporeans would litter, if they thought they could get away with it.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I find it very disappointing, frustrating and puzzling that a nation which has made so much progress and has such a well-educated population should have so many citizens with such a disregard for their surroundings.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is time for stronger measures to be implemented to drive home the message that littering will not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must have a sense of urgency to combating littering due to the surge in the number of dengue cases and the emergence of the Zika virus, both of which are transmitted by the Aedes mosquito.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Litter, especially plastics and cans, act as receptacles for water from our frequent rains and breed mosquitoes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amendment to expand the Community Volunteer (CV) scheme to allow NEA to appoint individuals as CVs will provide a boost to the headcount available for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Presently, only members of environmental-related societies or a council gazetted under the EPHA can apply to become CVs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, the amendment to explicitly appoint Auxiliary Police Officers as authorised officers will be useful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more eyes and ears on the ground, we are taking a step in the right direction to eradicate littering.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as our police and traffic police are equipped with cameras and recorders to support their enforcement work, all environmental officers and CVs should all also be similarly equipped.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will prevent abuse by offenders and reduce disputes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There had been some concerns over the selection criteria for CVs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry will ensure a stringent screening process to choose suitable candidates.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They must have the right public spirit, good communication skills and care deeply about our environment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Adequate training and periodic re-training should also be provided to keep our CVs updated.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This, together with the technology used, I believe, would address the concern raised by another Member of Parliament just now.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should be made to perform their work orders both at the place of the original offence and in the estates where they live.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The sense of responsibility towards one's environment must also be nurtured from young.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everyone must feel the sense of community ownership and the need to protect one's surroundings, and to keep it clean and liveable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I welcome the announcement by MOE to involve our students in the daily cleaning of our schools; it is being done in Japan and Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only will we inculcate the right attitude towards the environment in our young, they will also pick up real life skills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our students will also realise how difficult a cleaner's work can be and refrain from irresponsible behaviour such as littering.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They will also learn to respect the work and learn the value of work, regardless of whether they are white or blue collared.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, I would like to know how the authorities deal with those high-rise littering units when we cannot ascertain who in the family did the act.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another problem we all encounter frequently is that some HDB residents would leave rubbish in the public space around the rubbish chute, instead of disposing it properly or bringing it to the rubbish collection centre downstairs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think NEA and the relevant agencies should explore how to solve this problem.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree we should give the volunteers enforcement powers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also feel NEA should make efforts to use technology to improve their enforcement efficiency and avoid human errors as well as unnecessary disputes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, the enforcement officers could perhaps conduct their duties in plain clothes to achieve better outcomes and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One telling sign is that, if you hear someone asking, "Where is the rubbish bin?", then surely this person is a Singaporean!

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This remark proves that Singaporeans do have a very good habit of not littering.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They usually would look for a rubbish bin.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, what we want is that even when there are no rubbish bins around, we can still keep our environment clean and hygienic, just like the Japanese and the Taiwanese.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): We are capable of creating a new improved social norm where every Singaporean will take an active part to maintain an enjoyable common living space through the amendments of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In a densely populated city like ours, community living is all about respecting shared spaces and taking shared responsibility for the environment we live in.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the area of shared responsibilities, residents can do their part to influence and encourage one another to keep their estate clean, green and safe.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The authorities, on the other hand, must do their part to educate the community and enforce the laws when necessary to bring home the message that this Government will spare no effort to make our living environment pleasant for all.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Good neighbourliness is built upon soft skills, communication and care for the common spaces.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Allowing a resident to be able to penalise his or her fellow constituents now for alleged environmental infringements goes against what community living is all about.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure we have seen a fair share of neighbour disputes in our own constituencies involving alleged mosquito breeding, potted plants, cooking smell, cat feeding and so on.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Are we going to allow either party to escalate such disputes to a level where a person can take matters into his or her own hand by issuing summons to his neighbours or charging his neighbour for not providing proper identification on demand?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am deeply concerned that this Bill has the potential to make such disputes end in violence as the summons, deserving or not, will no longer be seen as coming from a neutral party.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The potential for such community conflicts to escalate beyond control in this instance cannot be ruled out.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is NEA losing the battle with litterbugs and dengue?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If it is about manpower, will the agency consider hiring retirees and part-timers on contract basis to assist?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I do understand that for some policies to be effective, education and enforcement must go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, using volunteers to educate fellow constituents through enforcement is certainly not the way to go because when the enforcement stops, the mosquitoes will return and so will the littering.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I urge NEA to tap on the volunteers to do more in the area of educating the public on environmental issues rather than to do more in the area of enforcement as appointed officers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While we need effective enforcement efforts, we also need soft skills to make the message stick in the mind of the people.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This, I believe, is more effective to combat environmental issues in the long run.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I support the Community Volunteer initiative by NEA to keep Singapore clean, green and safe, but we should leave the enforcement to the professionals.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I wish to seek clarifications from the Minister on the nature of this expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without expressed limits to the powers and without a specific regime, this Bill allows the Chief Executive of NEA to turn Community Volunteers (CVs) into functionaries of the state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I find this objectionable as it goes against the very spirit of involving CVs in public health and in environmental protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Its effectiveness in resolving public health and environmental issues is highly doubtful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the contrary, I would argue, it would undermine community ownership for these important issues in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When NEA launched the CV programme in 2013, it was envisioned that the programme will involve stakeholders, non-governmental organisations to encourage the community to take ownership of the environment and help tackle the littering problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Volunteers were trained to approach litterbugs and speak to litterbugs as fellow members of a community, as peers, fellow citizens or residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Though issued with NEA authority cards, the volunteers could only demand the particulars of uncooperative offenders to hand over the details to NEA officers who will then investigate the cases before prosecution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the limitation of authority was not just meant to safeguard the public interest but prevents any abuse of power or conflicts between citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was also the best way to secure community ownership through the powers of peer persuasion rather than the power to warn and punish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a leader of one of the stakeholder NGOs said, "The end game is not about us becoming pseudo police officers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The point is, we are trying to get more people to take more ownership of the environment so that when they see ordinary people asking others not to litter, when we start these conversations, eventually we can create a culture that is opposite of being indifferent." The key words here are "not pseudo police officers", "ordinary people", "conversations" and "create a new culture".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By all accounts, the CV programme has been successful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It goes to show that conversations between ordinary people evoking the morality of living in the same community work 99% of the time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only in 1% of the time did the volunteers have to act like pseudo police officers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this trend goes on, we would indeed create a new culture of caring for the environment which is why I find it very difficult to understand the necessity of giving the volunteers the full powers of an officer of the state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What exactly is the Government's justification, given the encouraging success of the CV programme in the first two years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it not an overkill to grant excessive powers to citizens to fine fellow citizens on the spot just because of 10 uncooperative litterbugs in the past two years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should not the Government allow the programme to run for a longer period before making any assessment of the necessity of appointing volunteers as auxiliary officers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a real danger that if the full powers are granted, we will indeed create a new culture; not a beneficial new culture of community ownership of the environmental issues and public health issues, but a new culture of antagonism between fellow citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NEA said it would provide the volunteers with the same training that regular NEA officers undergo but we need to understand that volunteers, as much as we should value them, come with a different set of motivation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NEA officers by virtue of their appointment and employment as an officer governed by clear organisational rules and culture will naturally be more circumspect in the use of their powers than enthusiastic volunteers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Already, a couple of the leaders of the stakeholder NGOs have made public statements that suggest that the new powers could be taken too far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One said that he was keen to see the powers extended to booking those who smoke in non-smoking areas and those who puff illegally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another said that he would like to see volunteers appointed as Block Ambassadors to police their own blocks of flats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where and when will volunteer auxiliary officers stop their policing of the community?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today is littering in the neighbourhood; tomorrow is proper recycling in the blue bins downstairs; the day after tomorrow is kids playing football in the void deck; and the next day, what neighbours do in their corridors, even inside their own homes, in the name of dengue eradication.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This looks like a slippery slope down the road to a police state where neighbours prey on each other and erode the mutual trust that we have painstakingly built up over the decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no evidence that we are experiencing a littering or spitting or illegal smoking emergency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The overwhelming majority of litterers just need reminding on the social norms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The study recommended outreach and communication strategies aimed at reminding people of the norms and getting specific groups, especially students and youths, to internalise the norms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The problem with depending heavily on enforcement and the threat of summonses is that people will litter if they do not see officers or other people around.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want them to internalise the norms and not litter even if they are alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Japanese had a 100 years' head-start over us since modernisation began with the Meiji Restoration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not want to undermine the development by fostering authoritarian culture of volunteers exercising powers over other citizens in the name of the state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to promote an environment of trust between neighbours, reminding each other to do the right thing, not instil fear and suspicion of each other if your neighbour is going to whip up his summons book because you were not mindful of the norms for one second.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will partially help tackle the littering problem in Singapore and is undoubtedly a positive step forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This, however, cannot be the only focus or the main focus of our efforts towards a clean Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Increased enforcement is important but perhaps, what is more important is a mindset change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What we need to focus on more is ownership of our living space and how everyone has an important part to play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In January this year, I gained experience as a Town Council cleaner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I worked with Hanif, one of our Nee Soon Town Council's cleaner and through this first-hand experience, it is clear to me that we are a cleaned city rather than a clean city.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I picked up so much litter that day: cigarette butts, cotton buds, tissue, condoms, nappies, the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After spending the morning cleaning an area, it was alarming to go back to the same area a few hours later to find it covered in litter again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The cleaners face an uphill task and almost an impossible task at times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These figures I believe are the tip of the iceberg and there are clearly more people who have littered but did not get caught.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this does not just become a cat-and-mouse game with the litterbugs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need a mindset change and this mindset change is important for our society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are often known as a fine society, as in a pay money fine city.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that fines are not the only way forward in shaping behaviours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope people are not avoiding littering only because they fear the fines or the corrective work order but rather because they know it harms the environment, because they know someone else has to pick up their litter, and because it is morally wrong to litter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that this sounds idealistic, but it is possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fundamental issue here is that residents do not feel that they are a part of the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If you see a piece of tissue paper in your own house, would you ignore it and walk by?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The answer is clearly no and that is because you want to make your own house clean and tidy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, why do we not translate this behaviour to our common areas?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to embark on more in-depth educational projects focused on the community instead of our usual nationwide Clean and Green campaigns that the public might be immune to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Research by the Duke University in the City of Durham in the USA showed that littering of cigarette butts was common at bus stops.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, the researchers decided to focus their efforts on reducing this problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They realised that large-scale events on anti-littering are not as effective as small community efforts targeted at hotspots of littering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The population at those large-scale events might not necessarily include that target group of people utilising the bus stops.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The engendering message is better received by putting in more effort on-site.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By using attention-grabbing posters, they were able to counter people's lack of sensitivity to the generic "do not litter" signs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They also passed out portable ash trays to commuters to remind them not to litter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not to say that we should use the same exact methodology to apply to Singapore as our patterns of littering might be different.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What I am advocating is we need to go beyond the clichÃ© environmental messaging and get creative.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another example of successful anti-littering campaign that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah mentioned earlier is the "Don't Mess with Texas – Real Texas Don't Litter" campaign in the USA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 1987, $2 million in tax revenue went to litter-picking and that cost was escalating 15-20% every year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After performing extensive research, they identified who the heavy litterers were.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are a pick-up driver, male, between 18 and 34 years old, who likes sports and country music, has an anti-authority disposition and is not motivated by appeals to civic duty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They were indifferent to the typical messaging about the environment and the cost of cleaning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, Texas decided to focus on these heavy litterers by appealing to their macho-ness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They realised they could succeed by associating littering with as being unmanly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Resources were pumped into getting popular country singers and athletes to do TV, radio advertisements and highway billboards to influence these litterers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The above is a good example of institutions thinking out of the box.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They knew their main culprits of littering would not care about civic duties and were anti-authority by nature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This goes to show that there must be creative campaigns we can do to reduce the rate of littering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, as mentioned earlier, research is also important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, it is something that they are calling for and have called for the past few years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some are not in total support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Allow me to respond to the points raised by them and for those that I cannot, I will do it during the clarification time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not to supplement NEA's enforcement headcount.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As I have mentioned just now, the primary role of the CV is to educate environmental offenders so that they are responsible for binning their trash.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That would be our primary goal where littering is concerned.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want to help them perform this role effectively and therefore we need to train our CVs; we need to give them certain powers so that they can perform their duties as volunteers as effectively as possible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Today, CVs do have to provide NEA with the details of offenders for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The experience of our volunteers under the existing CV programme found that the majority of litterbugs will comply when approached to pick up their litter without any need for further enforcement action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, when we need to enforce, the numbers are very small.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Such engagement and education have been effective so far and we will carry on this mode of deployment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For a start, what we want to do is to scope it to make sure that when we get newly recruited CVs, we will get them to adopt Bright Spots and then work with the local community to adopt and clean and improve the cleanliness and hygiene of the area through advocacy, outreach and educational activities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is how they would start; it is not about teaching them to enforce, getting them to enforce, getting them to issue summons and so forth.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As the CVs mature in their volunteering journey, the more experienced ones may even organise their own environmental activities and include enforcement patrols beyond Bright Spots, but this will take time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also mentioned the idea of empowering civilians with enforcement powers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is certainly not unique to Singapore; it has been done in many countries.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, in Singapore, Mr Pritam would also know that we have volunteer Police with enforcement powers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So far, they have carried out their duties very well; they are as good as our policemen; they are dressed like our policemen; they carry out police duties; they do not abuse their powers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Because, to the volunteers, it is important for them to uphold their duties, also as Singaporeans, in the intent of the act of the law.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But, unlike the Police Community Support Officers in the UK cited by Er Dr Lee, our CVs are not paid.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I know the new version of Police Community Support Officers will also not be paid and that is a great change in the way they are doing things.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our CVs, so far, are those who are passionate about the environment and are willing to step forward to take ownership of the environment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I agree though with the Members that good volunteers do not come on their own; we need to manage them, we need to affirm their contribution to the cause.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, training and monitoring will all be part of what we do with the volunteers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not just giving them a badge, giving them the powers to do whatever they want and then they start issuing tickets to their neighbours and friends.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is just an imagination of what could go wrong, but I do not believe Singaporeans would do that kind of thing.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will make a lot of efforts to recognise our CVs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will show them up in our media, feature them, the good things that they have been doing, For example, in the Sustainable Singapore Blueprint 2015, we have been highlighting the contributions of our CVs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we must explore more ways to make sure that their work is affirmed, valued and recognised by our community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee and Mr Gan also mentioned that there should be stringent screening criteria.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must ensure that we choose suitable individuals who have the right public spirit, good communication skills, as Assoc Prof Daniel Goh has mentioned, to ensure that the work they do is not the same work that our enforcement officers do, just to enforce.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They must be able to engage, to communicate and ensure that at the end of the day, they do this because together they can ensure everyone love the environment deeply.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Prior to joining the CV programme, we will properly screen and interview each individual to assess his interest and maturity towards environmental activities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will monitor what they do; if they have the propensity to issue summons almost every hour, certainly this is not the right kind of person that we should be deploying.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee and Mr Gan have also mentioned about equipping body-worn cameras to protect our CVs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These have helped to prevent abuse by offenders, protect our officers from allegations of unprofessional conduct, as well as remind our officers to abide by our operational protocol.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They may have done something wrong, maybe in a momentary lapse of judgement, they may have littered.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: When someone, a fellow citizen, comes and tells them, "please bin the litter", majority of them will pick it up and do exactly what they have been told.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Notwithstanding this, our CVs will be considered as public servants for the purposes of the Penal Code and exercising the power of enforcement and will be protected under the Protection from Harassment Act from any indecent, threatening, abusive or insulting behaviour or words when they are executing their duties, as I mentioned just now.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee, Mr Gan, Mr Louis, Assoc Prof Daniel, Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Png all mentioned about cultivating a sense of responsibility for the environment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I agree that the cleaning profession is tough and our cleaners face an uphill task in cleaning after us every day.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must have that respect for our cleaners and inculcate a sense of responsibility towards the environment and we, indeed, must begin this from young.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is one of the things that we are doing in addition to enlarging the space for people to volunteer and encourage people to keep the environment clean because it is their environment and it is their space.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: What criteria will new organisations need to fulfil?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, volunteers, if not managed, may abuse their powers, if not trained, if not supervised, may commit such offences.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, it is important for us to embrace them to make sure they are part of a strong team that can do this work well and pursue their interests in becoming environmental champions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Can these powers be conferred to the CEO of NEA?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Because, ultimately, if we have done it wrong, we have to be accountable to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: You can ask Parliamentary Questions; you can file a cut; you can move a Motion.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Then, we will divulge every incident that may be in question and be accountable for the act that we have done.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Members have asked how many volunteers we have in mind.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want them everywhere, particularly in areas where we want to convert to Bright Spots places where people usually litter or commit environmental offences.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want to put CVs there and make them a common presence for people to be noticed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: When we deploy these volunteers, we will not just be working with organisations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will be deploying them as individuals who want to work together and be managed by NEA.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA officers will be around to make sure that initially they are guided, they know their duties, they learn how to be deployed properly and, over time, with experience, we can leave them on their own.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If I heard him correctly, the Minister was suggesting that the scheme is really an expansion of the existing volunteer scheme and, therefore, the volunteers that come on-board will essentially be pursuing the same approach which they have done for the past three years, which is educative and to compel people to essentially stop doing what they are doing and, in the vast majority of cases, they will not be summoning.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If that is the case, is it necessary to have the Act allow volunteers to be extended enforcement powers?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have been consulting our volunteers on the ground.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They tell us that, apart from just being volunteers being deployed, being good citizens, it will be useful, in fact, it would be effective, if they do have those powers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we are concerned too that they may abuse their powers and, therefore, the synergy between the NEA enforcement officers and these volunteers is going to be key.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As what we are doing today, we have to train them, we have to monitor them, we have to supervise them, to make sure that they are reporting properly, filling up forms as officers should be doing, to ensure that at the end of the day, these powers are there for them to be able to use but not for them to abuse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, in the case of summoning, for example, potential law breakers, would there be an NEA officer accompanying the volunteer?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if so, should it not be appropriate that in the current circumstances to just allow the NEA officer to be the one issuing the summons and the volunteer just observing what is happening and assessing what the approach is?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That, indeed, will be how we will do it initially.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: When we deploy the volunteers, especially when they are new, we will deploy them in groups, in bright spots, not everywhere, not anywhere, not anytime, to make sure they are focusing on a particular area that they are trying to own and be part of it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over time, after being observed and observing the NEA officers, on assessment of the supervisors, people who are experienced, who assess that, yes, this group of people can be left on their own, over time, we will let them do it on their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is said in the Bill that the Chief Executive will have to do it in writing when giving the authorisation of the enforcement powers to the volunteers and would do it for every individual volunteer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This particular flexibility in which any or all of the powers can be given to any individual volunteer means that there is incredible flexibility on the part of the Chief Executive without clear criteria, without a clear regime, on what kind of powers can be accorded to an individual and on what circumstances?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Is there going to be a time-bound timing?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Is there going to be a place, and so forth?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Certainly, we expect our Chief Executive of NEA to be a responsible officer, not to just do whatever he thinks he can do because the Act empowers him.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There will be processes and procedures that he has to comply with and be answerable to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, there are at least two levels: the CEO and the Director-General.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And then, later on, deployment with the NEA officers to ensure that after they are trained, they are deployed properly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The CEO does not give a blanket power to every auxiliary officer to perform the duties that they want.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: He will be ascribed to particular areas that we want them to be effective in, in protecting our environment.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Keep your clarification short and on issues not clarified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I suggest that the Minister allow the process of volunteers following NEA officers to run its course before we consider giving volunteers enforcement powers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because the fact of the matter is it seems that, as most Members have suggested, the educative approach is really the way forward, and the Minister himself agrees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, perhaps, we can continue on that line and then re-assess whether powers need to be given to volunteers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second and very quick clarification: was there a public consultation done to invite feedback from the public as to whether volunteers should be extended enforcement powers?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: After running this programme for two to three years, and looking at and assessing outcomes, we are now doing a little bit more than what we have done in the past which was to merely educate, confine it to just some organisations and not expand it to everybody.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The process of allowing volunteers to follow NEA officers has already taken place and that is why we are implementing what we are implementing today.      .

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Workers' Party wishes to record its objection to clause 5.

speaker: The Chairman
text: How many Members wish to have their objection to clause 5 recorded?

speaker: The Chairman
text: [Hon Members Mr Low Thia Khiang, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Png Eng Huat, Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap, Mr Chen Show Mao, Mr Leon Perera, Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong raised their hands.]

speaker: The Chairman
text: Your objection will be recorded in the minutes.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.24 pm until 4.40 pm.
